content: The pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV10) includes polysaccharides from serotypes 1, 4, 5, 6B, 7F, 9V, 14, 18C, 19F, and 23F. These are conjugated to protein D from non-typable Haemophilus influenzae, except for serotype 18C, which is conjugated to tetanus toxoid (TT), and serotype 23F, which is conjugated to diphtheria toxoid (DT). For infants, the vaccination schedule involves three doses, which can be administered either as a 3+0 schedule (at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age) or as a 2+1 schedule (at 6 and 14 weeks, with a booster at 9–12 months). The Serum Institute of India produces a 10-valent PCV (Pneumosil), which is prequalified by the World Health Organization (WHO). This vaccine includes serotypes 1, 4, 5, 6A, 6B, 7F, 9V, 14, 19A, 19F, and 23F, conjugated to CRM197 protein. For infants, the recommended schedule is three doses at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age. Both PCV10 and PCV13 vaccines have demonstrated significant impacts in reducing pneumonia, vaccine-type invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD), and nasopharyngeal carriage of vaccine serotypes in various settings. These vaccines exhibit high immunogenicity and have been shown to reduce vaccine-type IPD, all-cause pneumonia, chest X-ray-confirmed pneumonia, and vaccine-type colonization, which contributes to herd immunity. The choice between PCV10 and PCV13 should be guided by programmatic factors, vaccine supply, cost, and the local prevalence of vaccine serotypes and antimicrobial resistance patterns. PCV13 may offer additional benefits in regions where serotypes 19A or 6C are significant contributors to disease burden. Although efficacy data for PCV10 from the Serum Institute of India (SII) are not yet available, its efficacy is expected to be comparable to PCV13 and PCV10 (GSK) based on immunogenicity data demonstrating non-inferiority. For Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccines, monovalent and combination formulations are available. Monovalent Hib vaccines are produced by manufacturers such as the Serum Institute of India, Sanofi Pasteur, and others. Combination vaccines, such as pentavalent (DTP-HepB-Hib) and hexavalent (DTP-HepB-Polio-Hib) formulations, are also widely used. These vaccines are administered in three doses, spaced four weeks apart, starting at six weeks of age. Several new vaccines are in development. Pfizer is advancing a 6-valent conjugate vaccine targeting serotypes Ia, Ib, II, III, IV, and V, conjugated to CRM197, which is currently in Phase 1/2 trials. Minervax is reformulating its protein vaccine candidate to improve global strain coverage, while Biovac is developing a 5–6-valent conjugate vaccine in preclinical stages. GSK’s trivalent conjugate vaccine candidate has been put on hold due to competition from higher-valency products and lower-than-expected immunogenicity in Phase 2 trials involving pregnant women. The WHO has coordinated the global Invasive Bacterial Vaccine-Preventable Disease (IB-VPD) Surveillance Network since 2009. This network standardizes the monitoring of the global burden and etiology of IB-VPDs, supports the introduction of PCVs, and evaluates their impact, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The network includes sentinel hospitals that report cases of suspected meningitis in children under five years of age. Laboratories perform confirmatory testing and strain characterization for Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningitidis using PCR and other methods. As of 2019, the network comprised 123 laboratories, including sentinel site, national, regional, and global reference laboratories. Surveillance officers at sentinel sites are responsible for assigning unique identifiers (UIDs) to cases, completing case investigation forms, collecting core data variables, and ensuring data quality. They must track cases with missing data, verify information, and update records weekly. Data from reference laboratories should be shared with clinicians, nurses, and hospital staff, as well as analyzed epidemiologically to inform stakeholders. The WHO South-East Asia Region has developed a comprehensive surveillance guide for vaccine-preventable diseases, emphasizing the importance of data quality and timely reporting. The guide highlights the need for collaboration between central data teams, surveillance officers, and laboratory staff to address data quality issues and improve surveillance systems.
